title: Device Models and Process Corners
intro: The SPICE MOS models from Level 1 to BSIM, how charge and temperature are modelled, and how process corners bound the spread (Razavi, Sections 17.3 and 17.4).

blocks.text: What a model is judged by

Accuracy in every region and for every geometry the designer uses, ease of extracting its parameters, and simulation speed. Analog design stresses the parts digital design ignores: the output conductance, the transitions between regions and the derivatives of current, which set gain and distortion.
Level 1 (Shichman-Hodges)

blocks.caption: Triode; in saturation the bracket becomes $(V_{GS}-V_{TH})^2$.

blocks.text: with $K_P = \mu C_{ox}$ and $V_{TH} = V_{TH0} + \gamma(\sqrt{2\phi_B - V_{BS}} - \sqrt{2\phi_B})$. No subthreshold conduction and no short-channel effects; reasonable for $L$ down to about 4 µm but poor for output impedance. Its capacitances avoid the abrupt jump at the triode edge (which upsets convergence) by blending:
Levels 2 and 3

Level 2 integrates the channel charge with a threshold that varies along the channel (the depletion charge grows toward the drain), so the current falls below the square law at large $V_{DS}$ and depends on $\gamma$ even at $V_{BS} = 0$. It computes $\lambda$ from the depletion width beyond pinch-off (with a patched formula to avoid discontinuities), includes vertical-field mobility reduction, threshold dependence on $L$ and velocity saturation, and models subthreshold current exponentially below a voltage $V_{on}$, with a slope kink at the joint. It is reasonable for wide, short devices around 0.7 µm, poor for narrow or long ones and for $r_O$.

Level 3 simplifies Level 2 with empirical constants for lengths near 1 µm: a threshold expression with short-channel, narrow-channel and DIBL terms, and a mobility with both vertical and lateral field factors, $\mu_1 = \mu_{eff}/(1 + \mu_{eff}V_{DS}/(v_{max}L))$. Its derivative of $I_D$ is discontinuous at the triode edge, so $r_O$ is badly predicted there.
BSIM and later models
BSIM gave up on purely physical equations and added many fitting parameters, with a geometry rule for each parameter:

items: BSIM (about 50 parameters): continuous currents and first derivatives between weak and strong inversion, substrate-dependent mobility, non-uniform doping. Weak for narrow, short devices; can predict negative $r_O$ at high $V_{DS}$.
BSIM2 (about 70): better $r_O$ through channel-length modulation and DIBL, but kinks in short, narrow devices.
BSIM3 (about 180 in version 3): back to physics-based equations; good to 0.25 µm in subthreshold and strong inversion, still weak on $r_O$.
BSIM4: fixes many of these and serves processes down to the 40 nm and 28 nm generations.
HSPICE Level 28 expresses parameters relative to a measured reference device, plus a cross term in $1/L$ and $1/W$.
EKV takes the bulk as the reference for all voltages, treats source and drain symmetrically, and uses a single current equation from weak to strong inversion.

blocks.text: Charge and capacitance

The simple (Meyer) capacitance model does not conserve charge: a simulator that integrates capacitor currents can slowly lose charge, so a MOS capacitor in a divider driven by a square wave shows a droop that is not real. Charge-based models compute the channel and depletion charges first and then partition them among the terminals. The fixed 2/3, 1/2 partitions are also poor for short channels; BSIM offers 40/60, 50/50 and 0/100 source/drain partitions.

Process corners

MOS parameters vary much more from wafer to wafer and lot to lot than bipolar ones, and gate delay can vary 2:1 with process and temperature. Foundries guarantee an envelope: they discard wafers whose NMOS or PMOS test structures fall outside a rectangle of speed, and supply models for its corners. Fast means thinner oxide and lower threshold.

blocks.text: Designers simulate every corner with supply and temperature extremes. Corners are built around digital speed, so analog quantities (offsets, matching) need separate statistical models.

blocks.title: Capacitance continuity
blocks.text: Show that the Level 1 blended expressions give the familiar values at the edge of saturation and at $V_{DS} = 0$.
solution: Edge ($V_{GS} - V_{DS} = V_{TH}$): $C_{GS}$'s fraction vanishes, giving $\frac{2}{3}WLC_{ox} + WC_{ov}$; for $C_{GD}$ the denominator equals $V_{ov}^2$, so the bracket is 0 and $C_{GD} = WC_{ov}$.
$V_{DS} = 0$: both brackets are $1 - V_{ov}^2/(4V_{ov}^2) = 3/4$, so $C_{GS} = C_{GD} = \frac{1}{2}WLC_{ox} + WC_{ov}$, the deep-triode split.
blocks.answer: Both limits match the simple model.

blocks.title: Geometry scaling of a parameter
blocks.text: A BSIM mobility has $\mu_0 = 400$, $\alpha_\mu = -20\ \mu\text{m}$ and $\beta_\mu = -10\ \mu\text{m}$ (in cm²/V·s units). Find $\mu$ for $W/L = 10/0.5$ and $10/2$ µm.

blocks.title: Mobility at temperature
blocks.text: How much does mobility fall from 300 K to 400 K, and what does that do to $g_m$ at fixed current in the square law?
solution: $g_m = \sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$ scales as $\sqrt{\mu}$: down to 0.81 of its room-temperature value.

blocks.title: Picking corners
blocks.text: A ring oscillator's frequency and a CMOS op amp's phase margin are to be verified. Which corners and conditions are worst for each?
solution: Ring: lowest frequency at SS, low supply, high temperature; highest at FF, high supply, low temperature (check both ends of the tuning range).

Phase margin: usually worst where the non-dominant poles move down relative to the unity-gain frequency, often FF (higher $g_m$, higher bandwidth) or a skewed corner; simulate all five corners at temperature and supply extremes rather than guess.
blocks.answer: Ring: SS/FF with supply and temperature; op amp: all corners, often FF or skewed.
